transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Aurora Head of ML), Priya Nair (Aurora Infra), Liam O'Connor (Aurora Product)

Auto Summary (auto gen, may be imperfect): Agreed hybrid SLOs; sample plan; Redwood to supply pricing and harness; Aurora to provide traffic sample.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, just to confirm audio, we have the agenda up — align on TTFT vs TPOT, sizing, and a benchmark/measurement plan for the POC.
[00:22] Samir: Yep, all good from our side. Our timeline is tight — we'd like a 4 week pilot that demonstrates we can hit p95/p99 targets without regressions.
[00:34] Maya: Great, we'll go through tradeoffs. Devon, want to kick off with TTFT definition?
[00:40] Devon: Sure. So TTFT — time to first token — is the latency SLO for initial responsiveness. TPOT we call time per token, which matters for longer generations. For our benchmarks we typically define both with p95 and p99 numbers and then weight them by traffic mix.
[01:05] Priya: Quick question — how do you handle caching? A lot of our calls will hit repeated prefixes, so prefix/KV cash could skew numbers.
[01:14] Devon: Yep, good point — we run both cold and warmed KV cache sweeps. The plan is to measure cold start (no cache), warmed prefix (KV warmed), and steady-state. We'll annotate the sample so you can see how much caching helps.
[01:32] Liam: For product, we care about perceived latency — so TTFT is more important for chat flows. For batch reports, TPOT matters because we do longer generations.
[01:43] Samir: Exactly. We're thinking TTFT p95 of 150–200ms and p99 of 350–400ms for short prompts (<64 tokens), TPOT p95 around 40ms/token and p99 80ms/token for mid-length (64–512). Is that realistic?
[02:03] Devon: Those are aggressive but plausible on dedicated infer for a quantized 7B-ish model with optimized kernels. On hosted, the p99 can be higher due to noisy neighbors unless you pick dedicated. Also model variant matters — we may fall back to a cheaper variant under load which changes quality.
[02:27] Maya: We should capture acceptance thresholds (both latency and quality). Samir, do you have an allowable quality regression threshold?
[02:35] Samir: We're comfortable up to 1.5% drop in our evaluation metric (ROUGE-ish classifier) during pilot; beyond that product will stop the test.
[02:45] Devon: Ok, we'll add quality monitors to the harness and run A/B comparisons to baseline.
[02:51] Priya: On sizing — our production estimate is ~1200 QPS peak, but typical is 200–250 RPS. Mixed short/long ratio roughly 70/30. We can share token histogram.
[03:05] Maya: Good. For the POC benchmark window we'll recommend synthetic traffic that matches that 70/30 mix, plus targeted bursts at 2x and 4x to test tail behavior.
[03:18] Liam: What about measuring TTFT vs TPOT under concurrency? If we push up concurrency, does TTFT degrade before TPOT?
[03:27] Devon: In our experience TTFT tends to hit tail latency due to scheduling and GPU warm-up, TPOT scales more linearly but per-token cost increases with higher batch sizes. We'll run concurrency sweeps and cross-plot TTFT p95/p99 vs throughput.
[03:44] Samir: Can you outline the benchmark steps end-to-end so we can map to calendar?
[03:49] Devon: Sure, proposed benchmark plan:
- Week 0 (prep): exchange traffic samples, confirm model variant, spin up dedicated pool or hosted config.
- Week 1: Cold-start and cache warm-up measurement; single-instance microbench (TTFT baseline).
- Week 2: Load sweeps (RPS increase) measuring TTFT/TPOT p50/p95/p99 and token cost; test quantization profiles and model variants.
- Week 3: Production-like replay with 7-day sample, burst tests (2x, 4x) and failure scenarios (model fallback, region failover).
- Week 4: Run final acceptance with the agreed thresholds and produce report + runbook.
[04:30] Priya: Ok that maps to our 4-week window if we start next week. We'll need an infra checklist for VPC peering and TLS certs.
[04:40] Maya: I'll send the VPC checklist and Redwood's onboarding doc. Also we include a small sandbox account to run initial microbenchmarks.
[04:48] Samir: On metrics — we need both client-side (TTFT seen by user) and server-side metrics (queue times, kernel times). Can you provide traces?
[04:58] Devon: Yes, we expose per-request traces, token timing breakdown, and cost-per-token. We'll include Grafana dashboards and a CSV export. Tracing may have slight timestamp jitter in the transcript but it's fine for measurement.
[05:12] Liam: How do we handle model rollouts? If we test quantized vs fp16, we need a canary plan so we don't regress quality.
[05:20] Devon: We'll do A/B canary runs in the harness with automatic regression detection. If metric drop >1.5% we'll flag a rollback. We'll include a manual sign-off step in the runbook.
[05:34] Samir: Regarding success criteria — list I'll give: TTFT p95 <= 200ms, TTFT p99 <= 400ms for <64 token flows; TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token, p99 <= 120ms/token for 64-512 tokens; overall quality regression <=1.5%. If we meet these under 1x production load we're green.
[05:57] Maya: That works as a starting SLO set. We'll record them as acceptance gating. Important to note we'll run both cold and warmed measurements and weight final acceptance by warmed steady-state 70% and cold 30% (or you can propose other weighting).
[06:16] Priya: Weighting seems fair but we want to see warm-state more. We propose 80% warmed, 20% cold.
[06:22] Samir: Fine with 80/20.
[06:24] Devon: Noted. We'll run 80% weighting on warmed metrics for acceptance.
[06:30] Liam: For sampling — how many samples per bucket do you need to get stable p99?
[06:36] Devon: p99 needs thousands of samples. For short flows aim for 100k requests aggregated across runs; for long flows maybe 20k due to cost. We'll run multiple iterations to get confidence intervals and bootstrap p99 estimates.
[06:53] Maya: Cost question — do you have an estimate for the benchmark run cost vs running production in Redwood Dedicated?
[07:00] Devon: We'll produce a preliminary cost estimate after we see your token distribution. Quantization and batching drastically change unit cost — we'll show low/med/high scenarios.
[07:10] Samir: Any security blockers? We need SOC2 attestation, SSO/SAML support, and KMS integration.
[07:18] Maya: Redwood supports SSO/SAML and KMS; we have SOC2 Type II. I'll attach the security pack. Private deployment options are available if you need air-gapped.
[07:29] Priya: We may prefer VPC peering for the pilot to keep data flows internal.
[07:34] Maya: VPC peering is fine — I'll include the network diagram and peering checklist.
[07:40] Liam: Let's talk about tail behavior — we saw some vendors have big p99 cliffs under burst. What's your mitigation?
[07:47] Devon: We use smart routing and fallback model variants — canary with smaller model, routing by latency SLO. Also auto-burst capacity on dedicated pools. In benchmark we'll simulate region failover and capacity constraints.
[08:02] Samir: For the harness, can we run the replay against our staging endpoint too? We want to validate integration.
[08:09] Devon: Yes, the harness can target staging or Redwood sandbox. It will capture per-request timings and output CSVs for your analysis.
[08:18] Maya: Quick aside: we noticed in your earlier note that some prompt types are extremely heavy — doc summarization and long context. How often are those?
[08:27] Samir: About 5% of traffic are >2k token sessions (heavy). Most are short. We'll mark those as "long tail" bucket for sampling.
[08:35] Devon: For those heavy tails we'll look at TPOT and cost per doc; we might recommend local batching or async worker flows to hide latency.
[08:45] Priya: On metrics exports, we want a daily CSV and raw trace export for the 7-day replay period.
[08:52] Maya: We'll include that in the runbook and set up a shared S3 bucket for exports.
[08:58] Liam: What about decision latency vs token throughput tradeoffs? If we push larger batch sizes to optimize cost we may increase TTFT.
[09:07] Devon: Exactly — batching increases throughput and lowers cost, but increases TTFT due to additional queuing. We'll show a Pareto frontier chart in the report so you can choose a latency vs cost point.
[09:20] Samir: For acceptance, do we gate on sustained throughput at peak? For instance support 1x production (1200 QPS) with SLOs, and survive 2x bursts degrading gracefully?
[09:32] Maya: We can gate on 1x sustained plus documented behavior at 2x bursts (e.g., graceful degradation with fallback). If degradation violates quality thresholds, then fail.
[09:42] Priya: Does Redwood provide token-level cost breakdown so we can map to our pricing model?
[09:48] Devon: Yes, per-token accounting and per-route breakdowns are included in the console and the benchmark CSV.
[09:55] Liam: Timing: when can we spin up the pilot infra?
[10:00] Maya: Assuming we get the traffic sample by 2026-11-24 and sign-off on model variant, we can spin a sandbox dedicated pool next week and begin microbenchmarks by 2026-11-29. Full run through to acceptance would conclude the week of 2026-12-27 roughly.
[10:17] Samir: That timeline aligns with our quarter end.
[10:22] Devon: One more note on measurement methodology — we'll use both synthetic and replay tests. Replay keeps request semantics but needs anonymization. Synthetic allows controlled stress. We'll correlate results.
[10:36] Priya: On anonymity — we'll hash PII and strip payloads, only tokens and timing needed.
[10:41] Maya: Great. We'll provide a template for anonymization.
[10:45] Samir: Are there standard dashboards you can share so stakeholders can monitor during the run?
[10:51] Devon: Yes, Grafana + CSV exports; we'll push temporary viewer links to your SSO.
[10:58] Liam: Any pitfalls from past pilots we should watch for?
[11:02] Devon: Two common gotchas: 1) mismatch between synthetic and replay—synthetic often underestimates tail; 2) prefix cache assumptions — if you warm cache in tests but not in prod you get overly optimistic numbers. We'll document both.
[11:16] Samir: Helpful. For acceptance report, include recommended production config (instance sizes, batching, quantization) and expected monthly token cost.
[11:25] Maya: We'll include that in the final runbook + cost scenarios.
[11:29] Priya: Could you also include a runbook section for incident response if we see model drift/quality drop?
[11:36] Devon: Yes — automatic alerts, rollback steps, and contact points.
[11:40] Maya: Ok let's capture the explicit acceptance thresholds now so they're in the record. Samir read them back?
[11:46] Samir: Sure: TTFT p95 <= 200ms, TTFT p99 <= 400ms for <64 tokens. TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token and p99 <= 120ms/token for 64–512 tokens. Quality regression <= 1.5%. Weighted acceptance: warmed 80%, cold 20%. Sampling: >=100k short flow samples, >=20k long flows.
[12:06] Devon: Got it, we'll build the harness to collect those numbers and produce CI style pass/fail.
[12:12] Maya: Any remaining blockers?
[12:15] Priya: ACLs for S3 export, and an NDA addendum for the anonymized replay.
[12:20] Maya: We'll attach legal doc template and security pack to the next email.
[12:24] Liam: OK, thanks. That was productive.
[12:27] Maya: Recap of next steps: I'll send pricing/VPC/security pack; Devon shares harness; Aurora sends traffic sample and confirmation of acceptance thresholds. We'll schedule kickoff for week of 2026-11-29.
[12:42] Samir: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[12:45] Maya: Thanks — talk soon.

Notes on transcription: occasional name mis-hearings (e.g., "KV cash" vs KV cache), filler words left in. Some speaker labels may have slight attribution errors.
